title: Carboprost: Hemorrhage Control and Bronchospasm Risk
bottomLine: Carboprost is a prostaglandin uterotonic used for selected postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony. Its major nursing safety issue is bronchospasm risk, so asthma or significant pulmonary disease must be recognized before administration and respiratory deterioration requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Used when uterine atony persists despite first-line measures and the obstetric hemorrhage plan calls for another uterotonic.
Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, fever, and flushing can occur.
Wheezing, marked dyspnea, or falling oxygenation after administration is not an expected nuisance effect.
priorities: Verify the hemorrhage indication and screen for asthma/pulmonary contraindications or precautions before administration.
Continue quantitative bleeding, uterine-tone, vital-sign, and perfusion assessment while the drug is given.
Escalate bronchospasm, persistent heavy bleeding, hypotension, or deteriorating mental status immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend uterine tone, quantified blood loss, BP, heart rate, oxygenation, respiratory symptoms, temperature, GI effects, and response to the full hemorrhage protocol.
interventions: Administer by the ordered route under the obstetric hemorrhage protocol and continue nonpharmacologic/other pharmacologic hemorrhage measures as indicated.
Prepare for transfusion, tranexamic acid, tamponade, procedure, or surgery when bleeding persists.
medicationSafety: Carboprost is not a routine choice in patients with asthma because prostaglandin F2-alpha activity can provoke bronchoconstriction.
Do not allow repeated uterotonic dosing to delay escalation for ongoing shock or a non-atony cause of bleeding.
teaching: Explain that transient GI symptoms may occur but breathing difficulty or worsening bleeding must be reported immediately.
delegationScope: Uterotonic administration and postpartum hemorrhage assessment follow state/facility LPN/LVN scope; unstable hemorrhage requires immediate RN/obstetric-team escalation.
examTrap: Giving carboprost reflexively to a patient with asthma without checking the respiratory risk.
oneLinePearl: Carboprost contracts the uterus but can also constrict the bronchi.

title: Misoprostol: Obstetric Use Requires the Right Context
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog with important obstetric uses under protocol, but pregnancy exposure can cause uterine contractions, abortion, preterm birth, and uterine rupture. Obstetric indication, route, gestational context, prior uterine surgery, and monitoring matter.
recognize: Obstetric protocols may use misoprostol for cervical ripening, pregnancy management, or postpartum hemorrhage, while the commercial ulcer-prevention label carries a pregnancy warning.
Uterine tachysystole, fetal heart-rate deterioration, severe abdominal pain, or excessive bleeding requires urgent review.
priorities: Verify that the order is for the intended obstetric indication and route rather than assuming the GI ulcer-prevention label applies to the obstetric protocol.
Review prior cesarean/uterine surgery and current fetal/uterine status as required by protocol.
Escalate tachysystole, fetal compromise, suspected rupture, or hemorrhage immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor uterine activity, fetal status when applicable, bleeding, pain, temperature, GI effects, and maternal vital signs according to the obstetric indication.
interventions: Follow the institution's obstetric misoprostol protocol exactly; route and timing vary by indication.
Prepare for emergency obstetric management if uterine rupture or severe hemorrhage is suspected.
medicationSafety: Do not treat misoprostol as a simple interchangeable uterotonic; indication and prior uterine surgery materially change risk.
The current U.S. label warns of abortion, preterm birth, birth defects, and uterine rupture with pregnancy exposure.
teaching: Explain the specific obstetric purpose and expected monitoring; patients using misoprostol for a nonobstetric indication must understand the pregnancy warning.
delegationScope: Obstetric misoprostol administration and fetal/uterine assessment require facility-defined competency and state-specific LPN/LVN scope.
examTrap: Assuming a medication's common GI indication defines how it is used in obstetrics.
oneLinePearl: With misoprostol, the indication and uterus matter as much as the drug name.
sourceBasis: ACOG obstetric induction and hemorrhage principles

title: Tranexamic Acid in Postpartum Hemorrhage
bottomLine: Tranexamic acid reduces fibrinolysis and may be used early as part of a postpartum hemorrhage response. It does not replace uterine massage, uterotonics, transfusion, source control, or surgery when those are needed.
recognize: TXA is an antifibrinolytic, not a uterotonic; it helps stabilize clot rather than directly contracting an atonic uterus.
Ongoing shock, concealed bleeding, laceration, retained tissue, or coagulopathy still requires cause-directed treatment.
priorities: Activate the hemorrhage pathway, quantify bleeding, assess perfusion, and administer TXA only under the obstetric protocol/order.
Continue simultaneous evaluation of tone, trauma, tissue, and coagulation causes.
Escalate persistent bleeding or shock regardless of temporary improvement.
assessMonitor: Trend blood loss, uterine tone, BP, heart rate, mental status, urine output, coagulation data when ordered, and thrombotic symptoms after stabilization.
interventions: Coordinate TXA with uterotonics, fluids/blood products, procedures, and surgical management as indicated.
Use the prescribed IV administration method and monitor the patient during administration.
medicationSafety: Rapid IV administration can cause hypotension with tranexamic acid products; follow product/protocol administration instructions.
History of active pathologic thrombosis or other contraindications requires clinician review.
redFlags: New chest pain/dyspnea or focal neurologic symptoms after stabilization
teaching: Explain that TXA is one component of hemorrhage treatment, not proof that the bleeding source has been controlled.
delegationScope: TXA administration during obstetric hemorrhage follows state/facility LPN/LVN IV scope and requires ongoing licensed assessment.
examTrap: Giving TXA and then delaying definitive treatment of a laceration, retained placenta, or uncontrolled atony.
oneLinePearl: TXA protects clot; it does not fix the bleeding source.

title: IV Labetalol in Severe Pregnancy Hypertension
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV labetalol is one medication used in acute severe hypertension during pregnancy/postpartum under obstetric protocol. Because it blocks beta receptors as well as alpha-1 receptors, bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, and bronchospasm risk must be considered.
recognize: Severe hypertension with headache, vision change, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea, neurologic symptoms, or other end-organ findings requires urgent obstetric evaluation.
Asthma/bronchospastic disease, marked bradycardia, heart block, or decompensated heart failure may make labetalol unsuitable.
priorities: Confirm BP using correct technique and follow the severe-hypertension protocol without unnecessary delay.
Assess pulse, respiratory history, perfusion, and symptoms before and during therapy.
Escalate persistent severe BP, neurologic change, pulmonary edema, fetal deterioration, or medication intolerance.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, heart rate/rhythm, respiratory status, symptoms of preeclampsia, maternal perfusion, and fetal status when applicable.
interventions: Administer by the ordered IV method with close hemodynamic monitoring.
Continue seizure-prevention and delivery-planning measures when indicated; BP treatment does not replace magnesium sulfate when seizure prophylaxis is required.
medicationSafety: Labetalol may cause symptomatic bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, or bronchospasm.
Compatibility must be checked before sharing IV lines with other medications.
redFlags: Persistent severe BP with neurologic symptoms
teaching: Explain that rapid treatment is intended to reduce maternal stroke and organ-injury risk while the underlying obstetric condition is addressed.
delegationScope: IV antihypertensive administration and severe-preeclampsia monitoring are governed by state/facility LPN/LVN scope and obstetric competency.
examTrap: Assuming magnesium sulfate is the treatment for severe blood pressure rather than seizure prevention.
oneLinePearl: Labetalol lowers pressure; keep watching pulse, lungs, and preeclampsia severity.
sourceBasis: ACOG acute severe hypertension in pregnancy guidance

title: IV Hydralazine in Severe Pregnancy Hypertension
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV hydralazine is another protocol-based option for acute severe pregnancy/postpartum hypertension. It is a direct vasodilator, so excessive hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache, and maternal-fetal perfusion changes require close monitoring.
recognize: Persistent severe BP is treated urgently because maternal stroke and other end-organ injury can occur.
Headache can reflect either preeclampsia severity or a medication adverse effect, so the whole clinical picture must be reassessed.
priorities: Verify severe BP and assess neurologic, respiratory, cardiac, renal, and obstetric symptoms.
Administer hydralazine under the severe-hypertension protocol and reassess BP/perfusion after each ordered step.
Escalate hypotension, persistent severe hypertension, pulmonary edema, neurologic deterioration, or fetal compromise.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pulse, symptoms, maternal perfusion, urine output, and fetal status when applicable.
interventions: Keep the patient appropriately positioned and minimize fall risk after vasodilation.
Continue the broader preeclampsia/eclampsia treatment plan rather than focusing on BP alone.
medicationSafety: Hydralazine can cause marked hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
IV administration should follow the product and facility protocol; do not repeat doses solely because the BP has not normalized instantly.
teaching: Explain that repeated BP and symptom assessments are necessary because treatment aims for safer pressure without causing hypoperfusion.
delegationScope: IV hydralazine administration and acute obstetric assessment require facility-defined competency and state-specific LPN/LVN scope.
examTrap: Driving the BP down aggressively without reassessing maternal and fetal perfusion.
oneLinePearl: Hydralazine vasodilates—lower the danger, not the perfusion.
sourceBasis: ACOG acute severe hypertension in pregnancy guidance

title: Dinoprostone: Cervical Ripening and Tachysystole
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Dinoprostone vaginal insert is used for cervical ripening near term under monitored obstetric care. Uterine tachysystole, hypertonicity, fetal distress, or active labor are reasons to remove the retrievable insert according to product instructions and protocol.
recognize: The insert releases prostaglandin E2 to promote cervical ripening and can increase uterine activity.
Concerning findings include excessive contraction frequency/duration, rising uterine tone, recurrent fetal decelerations, or other fetal distress.
priorities: Assess baseline fetal and uterine status and verify that induction criteria and contraindications have been reviewed.
Monitor uterine activity, fetal status, and cervical/labor progression.
Remove the insert and escalate when the product/protocol removal criteria are met.
assessMonitor: Trend fetal heart pattern, contraction frequency/duration, uterine resting tone when measurable, maternal vital signs, membrane status, and labor progression.
interventions: Keep the retrieval system accessible and follow positioning/activity instructions after placement.
Allow the required interval between removal and subsequent oxytocic therapy according to product labeling/protocol.
medicationSafety: Dinoprostone should be used only where continuous or frequent obstetric monitoring and emergency care are available.
Do not leave a retrievable insert in place during tachysystole or fetal distress when removal is indicated.
complications: Rare uterine rupture in high-risk contexts
teaching: Explain that fetal and contraction monitoring is expected because the medication can intensify uterine activity.
delegationScope: Insertion/removal and fetal-monitor interpretation require obstetric competency and state/facility-defined LPN/LVN scope.
examTrap: Treating dinoprostone like a passive cervical-softening product that does not require contraction/fetal monitoring.
oneLinePearl: Dinoprostone ripens the cervix, but the uterus and fetus set the safety limit.

title: Indomethacin in Preterm Labor: Gestational Limits Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Indomethacin is an NSAID sometimes used selectively for short-term tocolysis, but fetal renal dysfunction/oligohydramnios and premature ductus arteriosus constriction become important gestational-age risks. It is not a late-pregnancy routine tocolytic.
recognize: NSAID fetal renal effects can cause oligohydramnios beginning around mid-pregnancy, and ductal constriction risk becomes especially important later in gestation.
Maternal GI bleeding, renal dysfunction, platelet effects, and NSAID hypersensitivity also matter.
priorities: Verify gestational age, indication, planned duration, maternal renal/GI history, and fetal-fluid surveillance plan before administration.
Report decreasing amniotic fluid, new fetal concerns, GI bleeding, renal deterioration, or hypersensitivity.
Do not extend therapy beyond the obstetric plan because contractions continue without prescriber review.
assessMonitor: Monitor maternal GI/renal adverse effects, fetal status, and amniotic-fluid assessment when therapy duration/gestational age requires it.
interventions: Use only as part of a gestationally appropriate preterm-labor strategy; antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for neuroprotection, antibiotics, or delivery planning are separate decisions.
medicationSafety: Current NSAID labeling warns of fetal renal dysfunction/oligohydramnios from about 20 weeks and premature ductus arteriosus closure risk around 30 weeks and later.
Avoid concurrent NSAID duplication and review bleeding/renal risk.
teaching: Explain that this medication is time- and gestation-limited; do not self-treat pregnancy pain with NSAIDs without obstetric guidance.
delegationScope: Tocolytic administration/monitoring follows obstetric competency and state/facility LPN/LVN scope.
examTrap: Continuing indomethacin late in pregnancy because it previously reduced contractions.
oneLinePearl: Indomethacin's fetal risk changes with gestational age.

title: Penicillin G for Intrapartum GBS Prophylaxis
bottomLine: IV penicillin is the preferred intrapartum prophylaxis for patients who meet GBS prophylaxis criteria and do not have a contraindicating allergy. The goal is neonatal early-onset GBS prevention; needed obstetric interventions should not be delayed solely to complete a target duration of antibiotic exposure.
recognize: Indications include a positive late-pregnancy GBS culture and selected higher-risk situations such as prior newborn GBS disease or GBS bacteriuria during the pregnancy.
A prelabor cesarean with intact membranes is a key context in which routine GBS prophylaxis is not required solely for colonization.
priorities: Verify GBS status, allergy history/reaction phenotype, membrane/labor status, and the ordered prophylaxis plan.
Administer IV penicillin on schedule when indicated and monitor for hypersensitivity.
Do not delay medically necessary delivery or obstetric intervention solely to reach a specific antibiotic-duration target.
assessMonitor: Monitor maternal allergy/anaphylaxis signs, IV site, labor progress, temperature, and newborn risk communication to the pediatric team.
interventions: For reported penicillin allergy, follow the obstetric susceptibility/risk-based alternative pathway rather than substituting an arbitrary antibiotic.
medicationSafety: Penicillin can cause immediate anaphylaxis; verify the allergy history and maintain readiness to respond.
The potassium content and renal function may matter with high-dose penicillin G products in selected patients.
redFlags: Maternal fever with fetal tachycardia or other infection concern
teaching: Explain that intrapartum antibiotics reduce early-onset newborn GBS risk but do not eliminate every form of neonatal GBS disease.
delegationScope: IV antibiotic administration follows state/facility LPN/LVN scope; allergy assessment and obstetric changes require licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Delaying an indicated delivery procedure solely because four hours of GBS prophylaxis have not elapsed.
oneLinePearl: GBS prophylaxis protects the newborn, but it does not outrank necessary obstetric care.
sourceBasis: ACOG Prevention of Group B Streptococcal Early-Onset Disease in Newborns

title: Labor Opioid Agonist-Antagonists: Check Opioid Dependence
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mixed opioid agonist-antagonist analgesics used in labor can provide pain relief but may precipitate acute withdrawal in a patient who is physically dependent on full opioid agonists. Maternal sedation, respiratory status, fetal effects, and opioid-use history must be assessed before administration.
recognize: Recent opioid agonist therapy, opioid use disorder treatment, or chronic opioid exposure changes the safety profile of agonist-antagonist medications.
Maternal oversedation or respiratory depression can affect both maternal safety and fetal/newborn status.
priorities: Assess pain, sedation, respiratory rate, opioid-use/treatment history, labor stage, and fetal status before administration.
Avoid precipitating withdrawal by clarifying dependence and the ordered analgesia plan.
Escalate respiratory depression, acute withdrawal, or fetal deterioration promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, sedation, BP, pain response, fetal pattern when monitored, and newborn respiratory status after birth when exposure is relevant.
interventions: Use nonpharmacologic support and the individualized obstetric analgesia plan alongside medication.
Have opioid reversal/emergency support available according to policy.
medicationSafety: Mixed agonist-antagonists can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.
Sedating medications can compound respiratory depression.
teaching: Ask patients to disclose prescribed or nonprescribed opioid use and opioid-use-disorder treatment so analgesia can be chosen safely.
delegationScope: Labor analgesic administration and fetal-response monitoring follow state/facility LPN/LVN scope and obstetric competency.
examTrap: Giving an agonist-antagonist opioid without asking whether the patient is opioid-dependent.
oneLinePearl: In labor analgesia, opioid dependence can turn a pain drug into a withdrawal trigger.
sourceBasis: ACOG opioid use disorder in pregnancy principles

title: Epidural Analgesia: Pressure, Bladder, and Motor Block
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Neuraxial labor analgesia can produce hypotension, motor/sensory block, urinary retention, pruritus, nausea, or opioid-related respiratory depression depending on the regimen. Nursing priorities are maternal hemodynamics, fetal response, fall prevention, bladder care, and recognition of unusually high block or respiratory compromise.
recognize: Sympathetic blockade can lower maternal blood pressure and reduce uteroplacental perfusion.
Progressive numbness/weakness extending unusually high, dyspnea, difficulty speaking, severe hypotension, or marked respiratory depression requires emergency anesthesia/obstetric response.
priorities: Obtain/monitor maternal BP and fetal status according to the neuraxial protocol.
Assess sensory/motor function and do not allow unassisted ambulation when block persists.
Escalate severe hypotension, high block, respiratory depression, or persistent fetal deterioration immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pulse, respiratory rate, sedation, sensory/motor block, pain relief, bladder distention/voiding, pruritus, temperature, and fetal heart pattern.
interventions: Position and support circulation according to the obstetric/anesthesia plan and administer ordered fluids/vasopressors when indicated.
Use fall precautions and bladder management until normal function returns.
medicationSafety: Neuraxial opioid effects can include delayed respiratory depression depending on agent/regimen; follow the monitoring protocol.
Do not independently increase infusion settings outside the authorized role and protocol.
complications: Fetal intolerance secondary to maternal hypotension
teaching: Explain the need for assisted mobility and repeated BP/fetal checks even when pain relief is excellent.
delegationScope: Neuraxial infusion management and assessment are governed by anesthesia/obstetric policy and state-specific LPN/LVN scope; abnormal findings require immediate escalation.
examTrap: Letting a patient walk unassisted because pain is controlled while motor block and hypotension risk remain.
oneLinePearl: An epidural changes more than pain—watch pressure, legs, bladder, breathing, and fetus.
sourceBasis: American Society of Anesthesiologists obstetric anesthesia principles
